title: Hazards & Emergencies
summary: Mud, wet pavement, snow, ice, manhole covers, steel plates, and painted lane lines offer poor traction, so slow down, allow extra stopping distance, and slow further before curves.
On slick surfaces keep all inputs smooth, use both brakes gradually without fearing the front brake, and hold the clutch in to coast across a small slippery patch.
On wet roads ride in the tire tracks of vehicles ahead because oil builds up in the lane center, and near intersections, curves, and ramps stay clear of dirt and gravel at the road edge.
Avoid snow and ice; if you can't, stay upright, crawl across with your feet skimming the surface, don't brake until you're past the ice, and straddle-walk the bike if riding isn't practical.
If you must ride over an obstacle, slow down, stay upright, meet it at 90 degrees, roll on slightly just before it, and rise slightly off the seat, then pull off to check tires and rims.

Railroad tracks can be crossed at angles as sharp as 45 degrees without changing course, parallel trolley tracks and seams need a quick, sharp turn of at least 45 degrees, and grooves or gratings call for steady speed and direction.
Swerve by pressing the handgrip on the side you want to go, then the opposite grip to straighten, keeping your knees on the tank, letting the bike lean beneath you, and never braking mid-swerve.

For a quick stop use both brakes firmly and steadily, release the front brake at once and reapply it gently if the front wheel locks, keep a locked rear wheel locked if you're going straight, and straighten up before braking hard in a curve.
Face protection and proper clothing reduce injuries from insects and debris, and if you're struck, keep watching the road until you can stop safely, then check the bike for damage.

Try hard not to hit an animal, but in heavy traffic don't swerve into another lane to miss it, since hitting an animal is more survivable than hitting a vehicle; lose a chasing dog by downshifting, approaching slowly, then speeding away, and never kick at it.

If handling turns poor, suspect a tire: avoid sudden braking, ride straight, shift weight back for a front failure, stay seated with no weight shift for a rear one, and brake gradually with the good tire.

Twist a stuck throttle back and forth to free it, and if that fails, use the engine cut-off switch with the clutch pulled in; if the engine seizes, usually from low oil pressure, pull in the clutch and let the engine cool before restarting.

A wobble usually comes from improper loading, unsuitable accessories, or incorrect tire pressure; grip firmly, close the throttle, avoid braking or accelerating, and shift your weight forward and down.
Chain slippage often shows up first when accelerating hard or climbing hills, and if the chain breaks, close the throttle and brake gently to a stop at the road's edge.

questions.q: When riding on wet pavement, where in the lane does the manual recommend you ride?
options: In the center of the lane, away from both edges
Directly on the painted lane markings
In the tire tracks of vehicles ahead
Close to the edge of the road
questions.explanation: Oil dropped by passing vehicles builds up in the middle of the lane, so the tire tracks of the traffic ahead are the safer path on wet roads. Painted lines are slick, and dirt and gravel tend to gather along the road edge.

questions.q: Which braking method does the manual recommend on slippery surfaces?
options: Use only the rear brake, since the front brake is too risky on slick pavement
Use only the front brake, since it provides most of the stopping power
Apply both brakes hard and fast before you lose more traction
Use both brakes, applying them gradually
questions.explanation: Using both brakes is one of the manual's precautions for slick surfaces; the front brake can still be trusted, and building pressure gradually helps keep the wheels from locking and skidding.

questions.q: You cannot avoid riding over an ice-covered section of road. What does the manual advise?
options: Stay upright and go as slowly as possible, feet skimming the surface
Keep your normal speed so momentum carries you across the ice quickly
Lean the motorcycle slightly and keep both feet firmly on the footpegs
Brake steadily the whole way across so your speed stays as low as possible
questions.explanation: Stay straight up and crawl across with your feet lightly touching the surface so you can steady the bike if it starts to go down, and hold off braking until you are past the ice.

questions.q: A piece of lumber is lying in your lane, and you don't have the time or space to go around it. At what angle should you ride over it?
options: At a 45-degree angle
At a 90-degree angle
At a shallow angle so the tires ease onto it gradually
At a 30-degree angle
questions.explanation: When an obstacle can't be avoided, the manual says to meet it head-on at 90 degrees, with speed reduced and the motorcycle upright.

questions.q: As you ride over an obstacle you could not avoid, how should you position your body?
options: Stay firmly seated and lean back to keep the front wheel down
Lean forward over the tank with your elbows locked
Rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footpegs
Shift your weight onto the handlebars to keep the front tire planted
questions.explanation: Lifting slightly off the seat with your weight on the pegs lets your knees and elbows absorb the jolt and makes it less likely you'll be thrown from the motorcycle.

questions.q: Railroad tracks cross the road ahead at a 45-degree angle to your path. What does the manual recommend?
options: Change your path to cross at 90 degrees, since smaller angles are unsafe
Speed up and cross while the motorcycle is leaned over
Turn so you cross them at a very shallow angle, almost parallel to the rails
Keep to your normal path and cross; angles as sharp as 45 degrees are safe
questions.explanation: The manual says railroad tracks can be crossed safely at angles down to 45 degrees and discourages changing course to take them at 90 degrees, which can put you in oncoming traffic. Railroad tracks also appear in the manual's list of obstacles to meet at 90 degrees, but the part written specifically about tracks says not to change course for that.

questions.q: A trolley track or pavement seam runs parallel to your path, and you need to cross it. What should you do?
options: Make a quick, sharp turn across it at 45 degrees or more
Ease across it gradually at a shallow angle to avoid any sudden movement
Ride along on top of it until you reach the point where you want to turn
Speed up so the tires skip across it at any angle
questions.explanation: Parallel tracks and seams act as edge traps that can upset your balance and control, so cross them with a quick, sharp turn at 45 degrees or more.

questions.q: Your motorcycle begins to weave as you ride across a metal bridge grating. What should you do?
options: Hold your speed and direction and avoid sudden moves
Brake firmly right away to slow down before the weaving gets any worse
Accelerate hard so you spend as little time on the grating as possible
Change lanes to get off the grating and onto solid pavement sooner
questions.explanation: The weaving feeling from grooves and gratings is normally not dangerous as long as you avoid abrupt or extreme inputs and hold your speed and line until you reach solid pavement.

questions.q: According to the manual, how do you perform a swerve?
options: Lean your body toward the open space while holding the handlebars straight
Press the handgrip on the side you want to go, then press the opposite grip to straighten once past the hazard
Press the handgrip on the side opposite the direction you want to go, then let the motorcycle straighten on its own
Apply both brakes firmly while turning the handlebars toward the open space
questions.explanation: A little pressure on the grip toward your escape side makes the bike lean and change direction quickly, and pressure on the other grip brings it back. Let the motorcycle lean beneath you rather than leaning with it.

questions.q: You need to swerve around a hazard and also slow down. How should you handle braking?
options: Brake firmly during the swerve so you slow down while changing direction
Keep light, steady pressure on the rear brake throughout the swerve
Don't brake while swerving; do your braking before or after the swerve
Apply the front brake as the motorcycle begins to lean
questions.explanation: Braking in the middle of a swerve can cause a skid, so keep the two actions separate; the manual's illustrations show swerve-then-brake and brake-then-swerve.

questions.q: During a quick stop, your front wheel locks. What should you do?
options: Hold the front brake steady until the motorcycle stops
Release the front brake immediately, then reapply it gently
Release both brakes and coast to a stop
Press harder on the rear brake to balance the locked front wheel
questions.explanation: A locked front wheel has to be released right away; then squeeze the front brake back on gently so you keep slowing.

questions.q: While making a quick stop in a straight line, your rear wheel locks. What does the manual recommend?
options: Keep it locked until you come to a complete stop
Release the rear brake immediately, then gently reapply it
Release the rear brake fully and finish stopping with only the front brake
Pump the rear brake rapidly until the wheel begins turning again
questions.explanation: When you are traveling straight, leave a locked rear wheel locked until you stop; you can often still control the motorcycle in that situation.

questions.q: You must stop quickly while riding through a curve. If you have the chance, what should you do first?
options: Straighten the motorcycle, then brake firmly and steadily
Brake hard with the front brake while staying leaned over in the curve
Lean further into the curve and slow down using only the rear brake
Hold your lean angle and rely on downshifting alone to slow down
questions.explanation: Get the bike upright before braking hard. If there's no chance to straighten it, apply both brakes gradually and build pressure until you stop.

questions.q: A pebble thrown up by a passing vehicle strikes you in the face. What should you do?
options: Turn your head to see where it came from so you can avoid it next time
Stop right away where you are, even if you are still in a travel lane
Keep riding to your destination and inspect the motorcycle once you arrive
Keep focused on the road until you can stop safely, then check for damage
questions.explanation: Keep your attention on the road until a safe place to stop comes up; once you're off to the side, inspect the motorcycle and fix anything needed before riding on.

questions.q: In heavy, congested traffic, an animal runs into your lane. What does the manual recommend?
options: Swerve into the next lane, since hitting the animal is the bigger danger
Avoid it if you can, but don't swerve into another lane to do so
Hold your line and make no attempt to avoid it
Move into the oncoming lane if it has the most open space
questions.explanation: Make every effort to miss the animal, but in congested traffic don't swerve into a neighboring lane, because your odds of surviving are better against an animal than against another vehicle.

questions.q: A dog starts chasing your motorcycle. What does the manual recommend?
options: Kick at the dog when it gets close enough to keep it away from your leg
Accelerate hard as soon as you see the dog, before it can reach you
Downshift, approach it slowly, then speed up to leave it behind
Stop the motorcycle and wait for the dog to lose interest
questions.explanation: Kicking can cost you your balance and control. Instead, slow down and approach in a lower gear, then accelerate briskly once you reach the dog so you leave it behind.

questions.q: Your front tire fails while you are riding. How does the manual say you should shift your weight?
options: Forward, over the handlebars, to keep the front tire planted
Toward the rear of the motorcycle
Don't shift it at all; just remain seated
Stand up on the footpegs
questions.explanation: The manual recommends moving your weight toward the rear when the front tire fails: a front failure hurts steering and control, and shifting back adds balance and stability. For a rear tire failure, it says to stay seated without shifting your weight.

questions.q: Your rear tire goes flat while you are riding. After gripping the handlebars firmly and holding a straight course, how should you brake?
options: Apply both brakes hard
Apply the rear brake gradually
Use neither brake and coast to a stop
Apply the front brake gradually
questions.explanation: The manual's rule is to brake gradually with the tire that is still good. With a flat rear tire, the good tire is the front, so use the front brake. Avoid sudden braking, and as you slow, move carefully toward the road edge where it's safe to stop.

questions.q: Your throttle sticks while you are riding. What does the manual say to try first?
options: Roll the throttle back and forth a few times to try to free it
Check the throttle cable with one hand while you keep riding
Apply both brakes hard while leaving the clutch engaged
Continue at the stuck speed and have the throttle checked after the ride
questions.explanation: Rolling the throttle back and forth may free the cable and give you back control of the engine. Inspect the cable only after you are safely stopped, and don't ride on until the throttle works properly.

questions.q: Your throttle is stuck, and your first attempt to free it has not worked. What should you do next?
options: Keep riding at the stuck speed until you can exit the road
Use the engine cut-off switch without pulling in the clutch
Lock up the rear brake until the motorcycle stops
Hold the clutch in and use the engine cut-off switch
questions.explanation: Killing the engine with the cut-off switch while the clutch is pulled in takes power away from the rear wheel so you can regain control and stop safely.

questions.q: The front wheel and handlebars suddenly start shaking from side to side (a wobble). What should you do?
options: Accelerate smoothly to power your way out of the wobble
Hold the grips firmly and close the throttle, but don't brake
Brake firmly to stop as quickly as you can
Loosen your grip and let the handlebars shake until the wobble settles
questions.explanation: Speeding up makes a wobble worse, and braking can too, so hold the grips firmly and roll off the throttle to bring your speed down.

questions.q: To help regain control during a wobble, where should you shift your body weight?
options: As far back on the seat as possible
Up off the seat, standing on the footpegs
As far forward and as low as you can
Side to side, against the direction of the shaking
questions.explanation: Moving your weight as far forward and low as you can reduces the shaking and helps you regain control; then stop safely and look for the cause.

questions.q: You suddenly lose all power to the rear wheel, a sign that your chain has broken. What should you do?
options: Pull in the clutch and keep downshifting until you find a gear that still drives the wheel
Brake hard with the rear brake to stop right where you are
Close the throttle and brake gently to a stop at the edge of the road
Open the throttle further to see whether power to the wheel returns
questions.explanation: A broken chain cuts drive to the rear wheel instantly; close the throttle and brake gently as you move to the edge of the road to stop.

questions.q: Your engine seizes while you are riding. What should you do?
options: Apply the rear brake hard to lock the rear wheel
Downshift to a lower gear to free up the engine
Try to restart the engine right away while rolling
Pull in the clutch and hold it in
questions.explanation: Holding the clutch in separates the seized engine from the rear wheel. Once you're safely stopped, step away and let the engine cool before trying to restart.
